corrections.says: Neck (Bone-in), with a photo of thick marbled slabs
corrections.should: Trust the words on the card and not the picture, because a chicken neck is a slender skin-on cylinder about the width of a finger, while the photo shows chop-thick marbled pieces that look like pork neck bones.
corrections.why: Chicken necks are long and thin with almost no marbling, and the pictured pieces have the thickness and intramuscular fat of pork neck bones.

corrections.says: Thigh (Boneless or Bone-in); Bone-in Thigh; Boneless Thigh
corrections.should: Read the three thigh cards as one cut sold two ways, bone-in or boneless, not as three different cuts.
corrections.why: Bone-in and boneless thighs are the same muscle group with or without the bone, and the right-column Thigh card already names both forms before the bottom row repeats them.

corrections.should: Sauté the liver quickly and braise or simmer the gizzard, because the two organs need opposite treatment and the shared line does not say which method belongs to which.
corrections.why: The liver has almost no connective tissue and turns grainy when overcooked, while the gizzard is a tough working muscle whose connective tissue only softens with long moist cooking.

From snout to tail. Every cut has a purpose.

plates.footer: Better ingredients, better meals, a richer life

corrections.says: RIB drawn between LOIN and LEG HAM, at the hip
corrections.should: The rib section sits at the front of the loin, directly behind the shoulder and above the belly, and the band drawn at the hip is the sirloin end of the loin.
corrections.why: A hog's rib cage is in the front half of the body, so rib chops, rib roasts and baby back ribs all come from the blade end of the loin next to the shoulder, never from beside the leg.

corrections.should: Sliced fresh belly is not bacon; belly becomes bacon only after it is cured and usually smoked, and belly on a menu is fresh meat.
corrections.why: Calling raw belly slices bacon teaches a server to confuse a fresh cut with a cured product.

corrections.says: Pork Jowl (Grill) listed under Pork Belly
corrections.should: The jowl is the cheek of the pig and comes from the head, not the belly; it is cured as guanciale or jowl bacon, or braised.
corrections.why: The jowl is cut from the head, well forward of the shoulder, and no part of it is belly.

corrections.says: Spare Ribs (Grill/Braise) under the Rib section
corrections.should: Spare ribs are cut from the belly side of the rib cage, the lower ribs left after the loin and baby backs come off, so they belong with the belly while baby backs, rib chops and rib roast come from the loin.
corrections.why: In American butchery spare ribs are fabricated from the belly, which is why they are flatter and fattier than baby backs.

corrections.says: a Picnic Shoulder panel with Picnic Roast (Braise), Picnic Steak, Stuffed Picnic and Cubes, while the Shoulder panel already lists Picnic Shoulder (Roast)
corrections.should: The picnic is the lower half of the shoulder primal below the Boston butt, not a separate primal, so Picnic Shoulder and Picnic Roast are one cut that should appear once.
corrections.why: The shoulder splits into the Boston butt above and the picnic below, so the two panels repeat each other.

corrections.says: a second Belly panel with Bacon (Fry), Pork Belly (Roast), Lardons and Burnt Ends, under the same note as the Pork Belly panel
corrections.should: The belly is one primal shown twice under two names; Whole Belly and Pork Belly are the same cut, and Belly Slices and Bacon are the same product.
corrections.why: Both panels carry the identical note and repeat the same cuts under different names, so a trainee would count eight belly cuts where there are about four.

corrections.should: Burnt ends are a barbecue dish of cubed smoked meat, classically brisket point and sometimes pork belly, not a cut of the pig.
corrections.why: No butcher sells a cut called burnt ends; the name describes what the cook makes from the belly.

corrections.should: The trotter is the foot, cut off below the hock, and comes from all four legs; it is not part of the shank.
corrections.why: The shank ends at the hock joint, and the foot below it is its own item used for stock and gelatin.

corrections.says: Hock (Braise) and Knuckle (Braise) as two cuts
corrections.should: Knuckle is the British and German name for the hock, the joint where the leg meets the foot, as in pork knuckle or Schweinshaxe, so the panel prints one joint twice.
corrections.why: American butchers sell the lower shank joint as the hock, and the same piece is labeled knuckle in the United Kingdom and Germany.

corrections.says: Fore Shank drawn in the body wall between Brisket and Short Plate, under the Rib
corrections.should: The fore shank is the lower front leg, below the chuck and in front of the brisket, and the space behind the brisket under the ribs is the front of the short plate.
corrections.why: The shank is the leg that carries the animal, as the app's Shank card teaches, and no leg sits in the body wall where the map puts it.

corrections.says: Short Ribs (Braised) and Short Rib (Grilled, Braised) in one panel
corrections.should: Short ribs are one cut printed twice, so list them once, braised as the English cut in thick blocks and grilled as the flanken cut sawn thin across the bones.
corrections.why: The same cut appears under a singular and a plural name in the Short Plate panel, and the Lexicon already teaches the real split as English cut for braising and flanken for fast grilling.

corrections.should: Hanger steak belongs with skirt in the short plate, not the flank, since it is the thick central pillar of the diaphragm hanging from the last rib, one per animal.
corrections.why: The app's Hanger Steak card places it on the diaphragm between the last rib and the loin and its Skirt Steak card places the diaphragm in the plate, so the plate has moved a plate cut into the flank panel.

plates.title: Pacific Fish
plates.tagline: Cuts & flavor profiles. Fresh catches, timeless flavors, coast to table.
corners: From the Alaskan waters to the islands of the Pacific. Extraordinary fish, unforgettable flavor.
Pacific waters, bountiful flavors.
plates.footer: Save the ocean, support sustainable fisheries, good food, a brighter future.

corrections.should: Yellowfin has its own card lower on the plate, so this card should be bluefin alone rather than repeating yellowfin.
corrections.why: Bluefin and yellowfin are different fish with different fat, and the plate prints yellowfin twice with two different flavor lines.

corrections.should: Sablefish is soft, oily and velvety with a large silky flake, not firm.
corrections.why: Sablefish carries some of the highest fat of any Pacific fish, and the plate's own Black Cod card, which is the same fish, correctly says silky and buttery.

corrections.should: Black cod is another name for sablefish, which already has its own card on this plate, and Chilean sea bass is a different fish, so the subtitle is wrong and the two cards describe one fish.
corrections.why: Black cod and sablefish are the same species, Anoplopoma fimbria, while Chilean sea bass is Patagonian toothfish, Dissostichus eleginoides, from the Southern Ocean.

corrections.should: Rockfish is a small round fish sold whole or as fillets; it is not cut into steaks, belly or tail portions.
corrections.why: Market rockfish run a few pounds, and steaks are crosscuts of large fish such as salmon and halibut, so this cut list was copied from the large-fish template.

corrections.should: The first cut on the Albacore card is Loin, matching every other tuna card.
corrections.why: There is no fish cut called fiin, the block drawn is loin shaped, and loin is the thick top quadrant of large fish like tuna.

corrections.should: Yellowfin is the lean tuna, so its profile should read lean and meaty rather than rich.
corrections.why: Yellowfin carries little fat compared with bluefin, whose belly is marbled, and the app's own Tuna card says yellowfin is lean.

corrections.should: On the West Coast, Pacific red snapper is a market name for rockfish, which already has its own card; true red snapper is a Gulf of Mexico and Atlantic reef fish, not a Pacific one.
corrections.why: California allows several rockfish species to be sold as Pacific red snapper, while the name red snapper properly belongs to Lutjanus campechanus from the Gulf and Atlantic.

corrections.should: Flounder is a thin flatfish sold whole or as four fillets; it is too thin to yield steaks, belly, collar or tail portions.
corrections.why: Flat fish yield two fillets from the top and two from the bottom, and steaks are crosscuts reserved for thick large fish such as halibut.

corrections.should: The beak is the hard mouthpart that is cut out and thrown away, not a cut that is served; the edible parts are the tentacles and the body.
corrections.why: The beak is chitin and inedible, and it is removed with the eyes and ink sac when the octopus is cleaned.

plates.title: Atlantic Fish
plates.tagline: Cuts & Flavor Profiles. Fresh catches, timeless flavors, coast to table.
corners: From the cold north to the warm south, the Atlantic brings extraordinary fish and unforgettable flavor
Great fish, better meals

panels.title: The map
lines: From Cape Cod to the Caribbean
From the Gulf Stream to the Far North

plates.footer: The Atlantic provides, we enhance, you enjoy

corrections.should: Halibut is a very lean fish that tastes clean and mild and takes its richness from the sauce, so buttery misleads a server.
corrections.why: Halibut stores its fat in the liver rather than the flesh, and the Floor Deck says it has very little fat and leans on sauce for richness.

corrections.should: Tilapia is a farmed freshwater fish, not an Atlantic ocean fish, so the Atlantic tag is wrong.
corrections.why: Tilapia are African freshwater cichlids raised in ponds and tanks, and none of the tilapia in a fish case is caught at sea.

corrections.should: Tilapia is sold whole or as small skinless fillets, and steak, belly and collar are not tilapia cuts.
corrections.why: A market tilapia weighs one to two pounds and yields two small fillets, with no meat for a steak, a belly flap or a collar.

corrections.should: Grouper is a lean white fish with big firm flakes and a mild, faintly sweet flavor, not a rich one.
corrections.why: The Floor Deck teaches grouper as lean, firm white meat in big chunky flakes that is lean but holds moisture well.

corrections.should: Flounder is sold whole or as thin fillets, and it is too thin and small to give a steak or a collar.
corrections.why: A steak is a crosscut through the bone of a round bodied fish and a collar is the meaty arc behind the gills of a large fish, and a thin flatfish gives neither.

corrections.should: Plain sea bass names no single Atlantic fish, because in American service it usually means branzino, the European sea bass that is mostly farmed in the Mediterranean, while the wild Atlantic sea bass is the Black Sea Bass already on this plate.
corrections.why: The Floor Deck Branzino card says it is the Mediterranean one, usually farmed, and not black sea bass, the wild Atlantic fish.

corrections.should: Black sea bass is a lean, mild, sweet white fish with a fine flake and skin that sears crisp, not a rich or robust one.
corrections.why: It is a small fish of a few pounds prized for its clean, delicate flesh, and the Floor Deck teaches it as sweet and mild, firmer than branzino.

corrections.should: Scallops are sold as the adductor muscle, or whole in the shell with the roe, and the small side muscle is a tough tab that is peeled off and discarded rather than a cut that is served.
corrections.why: The Lexicon teaches that scallops are shucked at sea and sold as the adductor muscle alone, and the side muscle turns rubbery in the pan.

corrections.should: Scallops are bivalve shellfish, not fish, so a guest with a shellfish allergy must be told they are shellfish whatever the plate title says.
corrections.why: A scallop is a two shelled mollusk, and fish and shellfish are handled as separate allergens on the floor.

corrections.should: Shrimp are crustacean shellfish, not fish, and belong under shellfish for allergen and prep purposes.
corrections.why: Crustacean shellfish is its own FDA major allergen, separate from fish, and shrimp is the most common one.

corrections.should: Grouper is a lean, firm white fish with a mild, faintly sweet flavor and large chunky flakes, not a rich or buttery one.
corrections.why: The Floor Deck's Grouper card says it is lean but holds moisture well with a flavor that is mild and faintly sweet, and the Lexicon's Fatty vs. Lean Fish entry puts the reef white fish among the lean fish that store fat in the liver, not the flesh.

corrections.says: The card pictures a uniformly red snapper like the Red Snapper card.
corrections.should: Mutton snapper is olive on the back shading to rosy red on the sides, with a small black spot below the rear of the dorsal fin and blue lines on the face, so the black spot is the mark to look for at the case.
corrections.why: The drawing repeats the Red Snapper card and would teach a cook to identify mutton snapper by the wrong fish.

corrections.should: The Gulf Coast sea trout is the spotted seatrout, also called speckled trout, a silver drum with round black spots along the back and tail that is related to redfish and is not a true trout.
corrections.why: The Floor Deck's Trout card describes farmed rainbow trout, a freshwater salmonid, and the plate's name and drawing invite a cook to confuse the two.

corrections.says: Cuts: Head, Collar, Fillet, Tail; Flavor: Rich, firm, clean; Best prep: Grill, Bake, Pan sear
corrections.should: Tarpon is a catch and release game fish that is not sold, cut or cooked as food, so treat this card as a mistake and not as a table fish.
corrections.why: Tarpon flesh is bony and poor eating, there is no commercial tarpon fishery, and Florida allows possession only with a special tag for record attempts, so no fish case or restaurant carries it.

plates.title: Northwest Vegetables
plates.tagline: Local harvests, seasonal flavors, timeless traditions.
corners: From the coastline to the mountains and forests of the Pacific Northwest.
Same land, different seasons, endless flavors.
Local fields, forests, coastal waters, mountain valleys.

corrections.should: Northwest cabbage stands in the field and in storage through the winter, so the season should run September to March.
corrections.why: The plate's own Seasonal highlights box lists Cabbage under Winter while the card stops in November, and the Lexicon puts the cabbage family in the cold season's vegetable aisle, October to March in the north, with green cabbage built to sit in storage for months.

corrections.says: September to November, drawn as brown-capped cremini and portobello
corrections.should: The September to November window belongs to the Northwest's wild mushrooms such as chanterelle, porcini, matsutake and hedgehog; the cultivated cremini and portobello drawn on the card are farmed year round and have no season.
corrections.why: The card's art shows brown Agaricus caps with thick pale stems, and the Lexicon's Wild Mushrooms entry opens with the line that cultivated mushrooms have no season while the Floor Deck's Cremini card says it is farmed year round.

corrections.should: The card heading should read Fennel; there is no vegetable called tunnel.
corrections.why: The drawing shows white fennel bulbs with feathery fronds and the flavor line reads Anise, crisp, aromatic, the anethole scent the Lexicon's Fennel Bulb entry describes.

corrections.should: Leeks are a fall and winter crop in the Northwest, harvested from September into March, so the season should run September to March.
corrections.why: The plate's own Seasonal highlights box lists Leeks under Winter while the card stops in November, leeks are frost hardy and overwinter in Washington and Oregon fields, and the Kale card on the same plate already runs September to March.

corrections.should: Sweet potatoes are not a Northwest crop and do not belong on a plate whose region line is Washington, Oregon, Idaho and Montana.
corrections.why: Ipomoea batatas needs a long hot frost free season and warm soil, and the American crop comes from North Carolina, California, Mississippi and Louisiana, with no commercial acreage in the four Northwest states.

plates.title: Northwest Fruits
plates.tagline: Local harvests, seasonal flavors, timeless traditions.
corners: From the coastline to the mountains and forests of the Pacific Northwest.
Same land, different seasons, endless flavors.
Local fields, forests, coastal waters, mountain valleys.
Fresh, local, seasonal.
plates.footer: The Pacific Northwest, bountiful by nature.

corrections.should: Mountain huckleberries ripen from mid July through September, climbing with elevation and peaking in August, so the season reads July to September.
corrections.why: A season that begins and ends in the same month is a misprint, and the plate's own Wild Huckleberries card prints July to August for the same fruit.

corrections.should: Salmonberries are the first wild berry of the Northwest year, ripening from late May through June and finishing in early July on the coast, so the season reads May to July.
corrections.why: Rubus spectabilis fruits weeks ahead of the raspberries and blackberries the plate correctly places in July and August, and the bushes are picked bare by the time the plate says the season begins.

corrections.should: The fruit is spelled currants; a current is a flow of water or electricity.
corrections.why: The card draws red currants on their strigs, and the app's Fruit Atlas carries Redcurrant and Blackcurrant entries under that spelling.

corrections.should: The fourth flavor word is earthy; the printed Unthy is a garbled word and not a flavor.
corrections.why: Unthy is not an English word, and earthy is the only term from the plate's own flavor set that fits the letter shapes and the pattern of the other cards.

corrections.should: Blue and black elderberries in the Northwest ripen from late August into September, so the season reads August to September; June is when the plant flowers, not when it fruits.
corrections.why: The card draws dark black elderberries, which are a late summer and early fall fruit, and the only elderberry ripe in June is the red elderberry, which cooks avoid.

corrections.should: Ripe serviceberries, also called saskatoons, are dark purple blue with a dusty bloom and look like blueberries; the red-orange clusters drawn on the card look like mountain ash and should not be used to identify the fruit.
corrections.why: Amelanchier alnifolia ripens through red to a deep purple blue and is picked only at that stage, so a forager or server matching the picture would pick the wrong shrub.

corrections.should: Citrus is not a Northwest crop; the oranges, lemons and grapefruit on a Northwest menu are shipped in from California, Arizona, Texas, Florida or Mexico, and no inland or coastal citrus belt exists in Washington, Oregon, Idaho or Montana.
corrections.why: Citrus trees do not survive the winter freezes of any of the four states on the plate's map, and the only Northwest citrus is a few container grown Meyer lemons, which is not a harvest.

corrections.should: This is the same fruit as the Huckleberries card on the top row, and the plate carries one fruit under two names; every huckleberry sold in the Northwest is wild picked, since the plant has never been farmed commercially, so there is no farmed crop to set a wild one against.
corrections.why: Vaccinium membranaceum and its relatives resist cultivation, both cards carry the same tart, sweet, wild flavor words, and the two cards print overlapping seasons.

corrections.should: Huckleberries are dark purple, blue black or red and never golden orange; the drawing looks closer to sea buckthorn or cloudberries and should not be used to identify huckleberries.
corrections.why: The Huckleberries card on the top row shows the correct dark blue black berries, and no huckleberry species ripens yellow or orange.

corrections.should: Spring in the Northwest yields rhubarb, the first strawberries and salmonberries; cherries start in mid June and apricots not until July, so both belong under summer.
corrections.why: The plate's own cards print Cherries as June to July and Apricots as July to August, and the Northwest is a late region where nothing tree ripened is picked before June.

corrections.should: Winter in the Northwest means storage fruit such as apples, pears and kiwi plus frozen or dried berries; citrus is shipped in from other states and cranberries are a fall harvest, picked October to November on the Washington and Oregon coast.
corrections.why: The plate's own Cranberries card prints October to November, and citrus does not grow in the region at all.

plates.title: Southwest Vegetables
plates.tagline: Local harvests, seasonal flavors, timeless traditions.
plates.regionLine: Arizona, New Mexico, Utah, Colorado, Nevada
corners: From the deserts, mountains and river valleys to the rich soils of the Southwest. A region of bold flavors.
Same land, different seasons, endless flavors.
Local fields, desert grown, high elevation, river valleys.
Southwest vegetables. Bold flavors, deep roots, lasting traditions.

corrections.should: The Pueblo chile, the Mosco and Mirasol type grown around Pueblo, Colorado, is medium hot, hotter than a typical Hatch or Anaheim green chile, so read the profile as medium hot, earthy, meaty rather than mild.
corrections.why: Pueblo growers and Colorado State University put the Mosco at roughly 5,000 to 20,000 Scoville, several times the heat of an Anaheim and above the Big Jim Hatch, and the growers market it as hotter than Hatch.

corrections.should: The card is mislabeled and should read Potatoes, since the drawing is red and yellow potatoes and the August to November season and the hearty, earthy, versatile profile are potato facts.
corrections.why: Spinach is a tender cool season leaf, about 91 percent water in the Lexicon, that no one calls hearty or a storage crop, while the picture plainly shows tubers and the Southwest potato harvest in Colorado's San Luis Valley runs late summer into fall.

corrections.should: Arugula is peppery and nutty with a sharp mustard like bite, so read the profile as peppery, nutty, green rather than mild and sweet.
corrections.why: The Lexicon entry Arugula teaches that it is a brassica whose chewing releases isothiocyanates, the same reaction that sharpens mustard and horseradish, and only the youngest baby leaf is mild.

plates.title: Southwest Fruits
plates.tagline: Local harvests, seasonal flavors, timeless traditions.
corners: From the deserts, mountains and river valleys to the rich soils of the Southwest. A region of bold flavors.
Same land, different seasons, endless flavors.
Local fruits, desert grown, mountain fresh.

panels.title: States on the map
lines: Nevada, Utah, Colorado, California, Arizona, New Mexico, Texas

corrections.should: Prickly pear is mild and low in acid, floral and watermelon like rather than tart, so add lime when a dish needs acid.
corrections.why: The pulp sits near pH 5.5, well above the 4.6 line, which is why the app's own entry calls the flavor mild and floral and why anything canned must be acidified.

corrections.says: Desert Fig, Arizona, California, Honeyed, rich, slightly tart
corrections.should: There is no distinct fruit called desert fig; this card and the Fig card are the same Ficus carica from the same two states, so read them as one fruit.
corrections.why: The plate prints Fig (California, Arizona, sweet, honeyed, rich) as a separate card with the same illustration, states and flavor words, and the trade knows only one fig species in varieties such as Black Mission, Calimyrna, Brown Turkey and Kadota.

corrections.says: Mesquite, Southwest Deserts, Earthy, sweet, nutty
corrections.should: Mesquite is a legume pod that is dried and milled into a sweet flour, not a fruit served fresh, so describe it to guests as a native flour or sweetener.
corrections.why: The plate's own illustration shows dry bean pods beside a pile of ground meal, and the Prosopis pod is eaten only as milled flour or syrup.

corrections.says: Mango, Arizona, California, Sweet, juicy, tropical
corrections.should: Mango is not a Southwest crop; United States mangoes come from Florida, Hawaii and Puerto Rico, and the fruit on a Southwest menu is almost always imported from Mexico.
corrections.why: Mango is a frost tender tropical tree with no commercial orchards in Arizona and only a token planting in California's Coachella Valley.

corrections.should: Call this card Orange (Navel and Valencia), since those are orange varieties and tangerine, lemon and lime each have their own citrus card on the plate.
corrections.why: A card named Citrus overlaps the three other citrus cards and leaves a server unsure which fruit it means.

corrections.should: Joshua tree fruit is not a marketed produce item and no kitchen can source it, so treat this card as a historical desert food rather than a fruit you will see or serve.
corrections.why: The fruit of Yucca brevifolia is fibrous, has never entered the produce trade, and the tree is protected in California, so the sweet, melon like and crisp description matches no market fruit.

corrections.should: Washington is a Pacific Northwest state that is not on this plate's own map; Southwest cherries come from Utah and Colorado's high country.
corrections.why: The plate's map panel names Nevada, Utah, Colorado, California, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas, and Utah is among the top cherry states while Arizona's low deserts lack the winter chill cherries need.

corrections.should: Pecan is a tree nut, not a fruit, and belongs with nut and pantry material; its Texas and New Mexico origin is right.
corrections.why: It is the seed of a hickory, Carya illinoinensis, filed in the app under grains, pulses and seeds as one of the fattest nuts in use, and every kitchen stores and prices it as a nut.

corrections.should: Olives straight from the tree are bitter and inedible, so the briny, tangy flavor on this card describes cured olives, a savory pantry item rather than a fresh fruit.
corrections.why: Raw olives carry oleuropein, a phenolic so bitter it dries the mouth, and every olive ever eaten has been water, brine, lye or salt cured first.

corrections.says: Chile Pepper, New Mexico, Arizona, Spicy, smoky, bold
corrections.should: A chile is botanically a fruit but the kitchen buys, stores and cooks it as a vegetable and spice, so this is the one savory card on the plate and should never be offered to a guest as fruit.
corrections.why: The app files chiles under vegetables and under the herb and chile material, with the Hatch chile entry covering exactly this New Mexico crop.

corrections.should: Kiwifruit is a California crop from the Central Valley and Arizona has no commercial kiwi, so drop Arizona from the card.
corrections.why: The vine needs winter chill and cannot take desert heat, and nearly all United States kiwifruit is grown in California's San Joaquin and Sacramento valleys.

corrections.should: Oregon is a Pacific Northwest state that is not on this plate's own map; the boysenberry's Southwest home is California alone, where it was bred in Anaheim.
corrections.why: The plate's map panel does not include Oregon, so the (SW) tag teaches a wrong region.

plates.title: Midwest Vegetables
plates.tagline: Local harvests, seasonal flavors, timeless traditions.
plates.regionLine: Great Plains, Prairie Farmland, Rivers & Lakes
corners: From the fertile fields to the heartland, a celebration of Midwestern harvests
Good food grows here
Healthy soil, strong farms, bright futures

panels.title: The map
lines: States: N. Dakota, Minnesota, S. Dakota, Wisconsin, Michigan, Nebraska, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, Kansas, Missouri
Local fields, seasonal harvests, Midwestern pride

corrections.should: Midwest broccoli is not cut in April, when transplants are only going into the ground; the local heads arrive from about June, with the best crops in early summer and again in September and October after the heat passes.
corrections.why: Broccoli needs roughly two months from transplant to head and Midwest transplants go out after the soil thaws in April, so the first local heads come in June, and midsummer heat makes the buds loosen and bolt.

corrections.should: In the Midwest collards are cut from early summer until the ground freezes, roughly June through November or early December, and a harvest running to March is a Southern window, not a Midwestern one.
corrections.why: Collards take light frosts and sweeten after them, but Midwest fields in USDA zones 3 to 6 are frozen or under snow from December through March, so there is no field harvest in those months on the twelve states this plate maps.

corrections.should: Midwest kale is cut from June until the ground freezes, roughly December, sweetest after the first frosts, and the outdoor harvest does not carry through to March in this region.
corrections.why: Kale is the hardiest of the brassica greens and can be pulled from under early snow, but the frozen Midwest ground ends the field harvest by December, so a season ending in March describes the Southeast or the Pacific coast rather than the heartland.

corrections.should: Midwest spinach comes in two windows, spring from April to June and fall from September to October, with a gap in July and August when the heat makes it bolt.
corrections.why: Spinach is a cool weather leaf that flowers and turns bitter once days are long and hot, so Midwest growers stop cutting it in midsummer and local spinach should not be expected in July or August.

corrections.should: Acorn squash is the least sweet of the common winter squashes and its flesh runs fibrous and mildly nutty rather than sweet and dense, so the sweetness on the plate comes from the butter and maple baked in the cavity.
corrections.why: The Lexicon's Acorn Squash entry teaches that dry matter is around 12 percent, the flesh is fibrous and mildly nutty, and sugar never climbs the way it does in kabocha or delicata, declining rather than improving in storage.

corrections.should: Figs are a Mediterranean and California crop and not a Midwest harvest, so any fig on a Midwest menu is shipped in rather than picked locally.
corrections.why: The common fig is not winter hardy across the twelve states on the plate's own map, and the app's Lexicon places the crop in Turkey, Greece, Italy, Spain, the Levant and California, with no Midwest orchard or market crop.

corrections.should: Midwest black raspberries ripen from late June to mid July and are finished well before August, ahead of the red raspberries beside them.
corrections.why: Black raspberries carry a single early summer crop about two weeks ahead of summer red raspberries, and Ohio, the leading black raspberry state, picks from late June to mid July.

corrections.should: Plantains are a tropical cooking banana that cannot be grown in any Midwest state and have no Midwest season, so this card does not belong on a local harvest plate.
corrections.why: Plantain is a frost tender tropical plant whose United States crop comes from Puerto Rico, Hawaii and imports, and the app's Lexicon teaches it as a vegetable staple of West Africa, the Caribbean and Latin America.

plates.title: Northeastern Vegetables
plates.tagline: Local harvests, seasonal flavors, timeless traditions.
plates.regionLine: Atlantic Coast, Appalachian Mountains, Great Lakes
corners: From the fertile fields to the coastal farms of the Northeast, a region of rich harvests
Same land, different seasons, endless flavors
Northeastern Vegetables, fresh, local, seasonal

panels.title: The region
lines: Local fields, coastal waters, rich soil

plates.footer: Support local farms, eat seasonal, taste the Northeast

corrections.should: Cauliflower on a Northeastern plate should be credited to New York, which grows it in quantity for the fall market, keeping the October to November window.
corrections.why: The Northeast is the six New England states plus New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, and Virginia is a Southern state by the standard Census regions.

corrections.should: Celery on a Northeastern plate should be credited to New York, whose Orange County muck soils grow it from late summer into fall.
corrections.why: Michigan is a Midwestern state, not part of the Northeast, and the plate's own map does not include it.

corrections.should: Collards on a Northeastern plate should be credited to a Northeastern state such as New York or Pennsylvania, as a fall crop harvested from about September until the ground freezes and sweetened by the first frosts.
corrections.why: South Carolina is a Southern state, and a November to February field harvest is a Southern winter schedule that Northeastern fields, frozen by January, cannot keep.

corrections.says: OHIO printed three times on the map, with WEST VIRGINIA and VIRGINIA drawn inside the region
corrections.should: The Northeast is the six New England states plus New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, so Ohio, West Virginia and Virginia do not belong on the map and its state labels should not be taught.
corrections.why: Ohio is a Midwestern state and Virginia and West Virginia are Southern states by the standard Census regions, and the map prints Ohio at three different places, so its geography is unreliable.

corrections.should: Green beans on a Northeastern plate should be credited to New York or Pennsylvania, keeping the July to September window.
corrections.why: Michigan is a Midwestern state, not part of the Northeast, and New York is one of the country's largest snap bean growers with the same summer season.

corrections.says: SWEETCON, printed over a drawing of red and yellow onions
corrections.should: The card is Sweet Corn; its title is misspelled and its drawing shows onions rather than ears of corn, so read the facts as sweet corn and disregard the picture.
corrections.why: No ear or husk is drawn, the bulbs shown match the Onions card two rows above, and the facts (July to September, sweet, juicy, tender) describe corn, not onions.

corrections.should: The card should read Spinach; the printed name is garbled and names no vegetable.
corrections.why: The drawing is a bunch of spinach leaves, the facts (New York, April to June, mild, earthy, fresh) fit spring spinach, and the real Tomatoes card sits two places to the right.

plates.title: Northeastern Fruits
plates.tagline: Local harvests, seasonal flavors, timeless traditions.
plates.regionLine: Atlantic Coast, Appalachian Mountains, Great Lakes
corners: From the Atlantic Coast to the Appalachian Mountains, a region of rich harvests
Same land, different seasons, endless flavors
Local fruits, superior flavor, northern roots
The Northeast, where every season brings something sweet
plates.footer: Fresh fruits, local farms, coastal markets, seasonal harvests

corrections.should: Cranberries in the Northeast come from the bogs of Massachusetts and New Jersey, and Wisconsin, though it grows the most cranberries in the country, is a Midwestern state far from the Northeast.
corrections.why: Wisconsin borders Michigan, Minnesota, Iowa and Illinois and touches no Northeastern state, so the printed N.E. border qualifier is false, while New Jersey's Pine Barrens bogs are the region's second producer.

corrections.should: Northeastern cherries come from New York and Pennsylvania, and Michigan is a Midwestern state that shares no border with the Northeast.
corrections.why: Michigan borders Ohio, Indiana and Wisconsin, with Ohio between it and Pennsylvania, so the printed N.E. border qualifier is invented, while Pennsylvania's Adams County is a real cherry district on the plate's own map.

corrections.should: Plums in the Northeast come from New York, Pennsylvania and New Jersey orchards, and Michigan is a Midwestern state outside this plate's region.
corrections.why: Michigan is not one of the twelve states on the plate's own map, while New Jersey grows plums in the same stone fruit belt as its peaches.

corrections.should: Figs are not a Northeastern farm crop; fresh figs on a Northeast menu come from California's Central Valley or are imported, and in New York the fig is only a backyard tree that must be wrapped or buried to survive winter.
corrections.why: Northeastern California is cold high desert that grows no figs, so California (N.E. regions) is a garbled location, and the fig tree is not winter hardy in New York, so there is no commercial New York crop.

corrections.should: Northeastern grapes come from New York (Finger Lakes, Lake Erie and Long Island), Pennsylvania (the Lake Erie Concord belt) and New Jersey, and Virginia is a Southern state outside the plate's region.
corrections.why: Virginia does not appear on the plate's own map, which ends at Maryland, while New Jersey has an established grape and wine industry in the Outer Coastal Plain.

corrections.should: Pomegranates are not a Northeastern crop; the ones on a Northeast menu come from California's San Joaquin Valley, harvested in the fall, and New Jersey has no commercial pomegranate orchards.
corrections.why: The pomegranate needs long hot dry summers and mild winters that New Jersey does not have, and northeastern California is cold high desert with no pomegranate orchards, so both printed locations are wrong.

corrections.should: The fuzzy brown kiwifruit pictured is a California crop or an import from New Zealand, Italy and Chile; the only kiwi grown in the Northeast is the small smooth skinned hardy kiwi, raised on a few farms in Pennsylvania, New York and New England.
corrections.why: Fuzzy kiwifruit (Actinidia deliciosa) is not winter hardy in New York or Pennsylvania and has no commercial acreage there, while the grape sized hardy kiwi (Actinidia arguta) is a different fruit that does not match the plate's illustration.

corrections.should: No citrus grows in the Northeast; the oranges, lemons and grapefruit on a Northeast menu are shipped in from Florida, California and Texas and are not a local Northeastern fruit.
corrections.why: Citrus trees cannot survive Northeastern winters, and Florida's northeast coast is a Southern location, so the plate's own printed source confirms this is not a regional fruit.

corrections.should: The large orange persimmons pictured are the Asian Fuyu and Hachiya types grown in California; only the small wild American persimmon reaches southern Pennsylvania and New Jersey, and the three states printed are all Southern states outside this plate's region.
corrections.why: Virginia, Tennessee and North Carolina are not Northeastern states and do not appear on the plate's map, and the Asian persimmon (Diospyros kaki) illustrated is a California crop, not a Northeastern one.

Good food grows here

items.name: Okra
facts: Grassy, vegetal, mildly sweet, distinctive mucilaginous texture (technically a fruit, culinary a vegetable)

panels.title: Flavor profile key
lines: Note: Okra is a fruit botanically, but is culinarily treated as a vegetable.

plates.footer: Local harvests, Southern traditions, seasonal flavors

corrections.should: Fresh Southern peas in Georgia, South Carolina and Alabama come in from about June through September.
corrections.why: Cowpeas are sown only after the last frost and need 60 to 90 days to reach the green shell stage, so the fresh crop arrives in early summer and runs into September rather than starting in May.

corrections.should: Broccoli's Where line should name Southeastern states only, such as Georgia, Florida and North Carolina.
corrections.why: California is on the West Coast and lies outside the Gulf South, Atlantic Coast and Appalachia that the plate's own region line and map define, while every other box names only Southeastern states.

plates.title: Southeastern Fruits
plates.tagline: Bold flavors, rich traditions, fresh from the region. Seasonal harvests, local farms, coastal to Appalachian.
plates.regionLine: Kentucky, Tennessee, North Carolina, South Carolina, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, Florida
corners: From the Gulf Coast to the Appalachians and beyond
Same land, different seasons, endless flavors
plates.footer: Local harvests, seasonal flavors. The Southeast, always in season.

corrections.says: Pecans, listed among the fruits, Georgia, October to November
corrections.should: Pecans are a nut, not a fruit, so treat this tile as the region's nut even though Georgia and the October to November harvest are correct.
corrections.why: In the kitchen pecans are shelled, toasted and handled with walnuts and almonds, and the app's Lexicon files pecan in the nut and seed atlas as one of the fattest nuts in use at around 72 percent oil.

corrections.says: Magnolias (Sweetbay), Southeast, Spring, Flavor Citrus, Floral, Creamy
corrections.should: Sweetbay magnolia is a flower, not a fruit; its petals can be pickled or used as a gingery garnish and its leaves stand in for bay, but no magnolia fruit is eaten.
corrections.why: The tile illustrates and names the blossom, and the tree's actual fruit is a woody cone of red seeds with no culinary use.

corrections.should: Pineapple is not a commercial Florida crop today; fresh pineapple on a Southeastern menu is imported, mostly from Costa Rica, with Hawaii the only United States producer.
corrections.why: Florida's Indian River pineapple industry ended about a century ago and survives only in backyards, so a cook should not source or season it as Floridian.

corrections.should: Florida avocados are in season from about June through January, not year-round; the year-round supply on most menus is Hass from Mexico and California.
corrections.why: Florida grows the green-skin West Indian and Guatemalan types, which are harvested from early summer into winter with nothing from Florida in spring.

corrections.should: Pomegranates in the United States are a California crop harvested September through December; Southeastern plantings are small trial orchards with no commercial supply a kitchen could buy locally.
corrections.why: Well over nine tenths of American pomegranates come from California's San Joaquin Valley, and the humid Southeast is a marginal, disease-prone site for the fruit.

corrections.should: Kiwifruit is not a Florida crop; American kiwi is grown in California and picked in October and November, with only small plantings in Georgia and Alabama, and the November to April window is the cold-stored and imported supply season.
corrections.why: Fuzzy kiwi needs hundreds of winter chill hours that Florida cannot supply, and the Lexicon notes kiwi is climacteric and picked hard, which is why stored fruit sells all winter regardless of where it grew.

corrections.should: Cranberries are not a Southeastern crop; the United States harvest comes from cold northern bogs in Wisconsin, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Oregon and Washington, picked September to November.
corrections.why: Cranberries need cold winters and acidic bog conditions the Southeast does not have, and none of the nine states on the plate's own region line has commercial cranberry bogs.

corrections.should: Florida carambola fruits from about June through February in two flushes, late summer and midwinter, so the winter crop is the larger one and May is too early.
corrections.why: Florida is the right region, but spring is the leanest time for South Florida carambola trees, the opposite of what the plate prints.

plates.title: Culinary Spices
plates.tagline: Flavor, aroma, tradition, global cuisine.
corners: Small ingredients... Big flavors around the world
Different cultures, different spices, same table
The right spice doesn't just season your food... it brings it to life.
plates.footer: Good food, good spices, a richer life

corrections.says: Green Pepper / Flavor: Fresh, citrusy, mild / Use: Salads, vegetables, fish
corrections.should: The card shows green peppercorns, the unripe berry of the black pepper vine sold brined or freeze dried, so it should be named Green Peppercorn; in an American kitchen green pepper means a green bell pepper.
corrections.why: The picture is a bowl of small round green berries beside black and white peppercorns, and the app's Black Pepper and the Pepper Family entry defines green pepper as the unripe berry, fresh and bright, used in steak au poivre vert.

corrections.should: Plain paprika is sweet, fruity and mild but not smoky; only Spanish smoked paprika (pimenton de la Vera) tastes of smoke, so the card should say sweet, fruity, mild or name the smoked kind.
corrections.why: Sweet and Hungarian paprika are air dried ground red peppers with no smoke flavor, and the app's Paprika and Pimenton entry keeps the oak smoked Spanish style separate from the bright, fruity Hungarian kind.

corrections.says: Sweet Basil / Flavor: Sweet, spicy, fresh / Use: Italian, pasta, salads
corrections.should: Sweet basil is the same herb as the Basil card in row 3 (Ocimum basilicum, the common Genovese basil), so the plate lists one herb twice under two names; keep one basil card, or make the second card Thai basil, a different anise scented plant.
corrections.why: Sweet basil is the standard trade and botanical name for ordinary culinary basil, both cards draw the same broad green leaf and give nearly the same uses, and the app's Thai Basil entry uses sweet basil as the plain name for Genovese basil.

corrections.says: Anise, drawn as eight pointed star shaped pods
corrections.should: The picture is star anise, the pod of the Asian tree Illicium verum, a different plant from anise seed; name the card Star Anise, or keep the name Anise and draw the small oval seed of Pimpinella anisum.
corrections.why: Anise seed is the small gray green Mediterranean seed of pastis, ouzo and pizzelle while star anise is the eight pointed pod of pho, red braised pork and five spice, and the app keeps them as two separate Lexicon entries that share anethole but not personality.

corrections.says: Harissa, drawn as a red paste in a bowl, among the dry spices
corrections.should: Harissa is a Tunisian chili paste of dried chilies pounded with garlic, salt and toasted spices and kept under olive oil, a condiment rather than a dry spice; if a dry blend is meant, call it harissa spice blend.
corrections.why: The card draws a wet red paste, and the app's Lexicon and Floor Deck both file harissa as a Tunisian red paste of dried chilies, garlic and toasted caraway, coriander and cumin finished under oil.

plates.title: The World of Culinary Mushrooms
plates.tagline: Flavor profiles, culinary uses, a gastronomic journey.
corners: Small fungi, big flavor
The right mushroom transforms a dish. Different forests, different flavors. Same extraordinary experience.

items.name: Enoki
facts: Hot pots, salads, stir-fries, soups, noodles

items.name: Wood Ear
facts: Stir-fries, soups, salads, noodles, hot pots

plates.footer: Good ingredients, better meals, a richer life

corrections.should: The cultivated enoki sold in shops is Flammulina filiformis, split in 2018 from the European velvet shank Flammulina velutipes, a close cousin rather than the same mushroom.
corrections.why: The app's Lexicon entry for Enoki opens with Flammulina filiformis and names the 2018 split from the European velvet shank.

corrections.should: Most dried black wood ear a kitchen buys is Auricularia heimuer, named in 2014 and long sold under the name of the European jelly ear, Auricularia auricula-judae, and cloud ear is Auricularia cornea.
corrections.why: The app's Lexicon entry for Wood Ear teaches that the Chinese dried product is Auricularia heimuer and that Auricularia auricula-judae is the elder European jelly ear.

corrections.says: Illustrated as an orange cluster of tiered, fan shaped shelves
corrections.should: A lobster mushroom is a single lumpy, distorted red orange body with white flesh, because Hypomyces lactifluorum is a mold that grows over a Russula or Lactarius and deforms it, so the drawing shows a bracket fungus such as chicken of the woods, not a lobster mushroom.
corrections.why: The panel draws tiered orange fans, which is the form of chicken of the woods (Laetiporus), and a cook would learn the wrong shape to recognize at the market.

corrections.says: Hen of the Woods (Grifola frondosa): earthy, woodsy, rich
corrections.should: Hen of the woods and maitake are one mushroom, Grifola frondosa, so this panel repeats the Maitake panel under a second name and should be read as the same entry.
corrections.why: Both panels print the identical Latin name Grifola frondosa, and the app's Lexicon entry for Maitake opens with Grifola frondosa, hen of the woods, yet the plate gives the one mushroom two flavor profiles (delicate in one panel, rich in the other).

corrections.should: The mushroom with the Latin name Sparassis crispa is the cauliflower mushroom, and Chorioleus is not a real mushroom name.
corrections.why: Sparassis crispa is sold and foraged everywhere as the cauliflower mushroom, its ruffled pale cluster is what the panel draws, and no genus, species or trade name called Chorioleus exists.

plates.title: The World's Great Cheeses
plates.tagline: Tradition, terroir, time.
corners: Iconic cheeses of the world

panels.title: Cheese categories
lines: Soft cheeses: Creamy, mild, spreadable. Brie, Camembert, Goat Cheese
Semi-soft cheeses: Smooth, rich, flexible. Havarti, Gouda, Taleggio
Hard cheeses: Firm, aged, complex. Parmigiano Reggiano, Comté, Cheddar
Blue cheeses: Bold, pungent, distinctive. Roquefort, Gorgonzola, Stilton
Fresh cheeses: Light, delicate, clean. Mozzarella, Feta, Ricotta

plates.footer: Exceptional cheeses, extraordinary places, unforgettable flavors

corrections.should: Comté is a firm, nutty, aged Alpine cheese with no blue veining, so the style line should read something like nutty, firm, complex.
corrections.why: Comté is a pressed cooked hard cheese, the plate's own Cheese Categories panel files it under Hard cheeses, the wedge pictured is a plain firm cheese, and the line simply repeats the Roquefort card with tangy misprinted as tarity.

corrections.should: Époisses is a washed rind cheese and is never smoked, so smoky should be replaced with a word like meaty or salty.
corrections.why: Époisses de Bourgogne is washed with brine and marc de Bourgogne, and the app's own deck describes the washed rind family as brine or booze washed and stinky, never smoked.

corrections.says: Pictured as a bright orange crumbly block
corrections.should: Parmigiano Reggiano has a pale straw yellow paste with a crystalline grain, and the orange block pictured looks like colored cheddar.
corrections.why: Parmigiano Reggiano is never colored with annatto, so its paste is straw colored and the picture would mislead a server at the counter.

corrections.says: Blue Shropshire, pictured with a white paste
corrections.should: The cheese is called Shropshire Blue, and its paste is orange from annatto with blue veins rather than the white paste shown.
corrections.why: Shropshire Blue is the name used by every maker, and it is an annatto tinted Stilton style blue, so both the reversed name and the white paste picture would teach a server to misname and misidentify it.

plates.title: The World of Charcuterie & Dried Meats
plates.tagline: Tradition, craft, flavor, culture. Preserved by time. Perfected by tradition.

items.name: Prosciutto
facts: Air-cured ham, delicate, silky, slightly sweet

items.name: Salumi Misti
facts: Mixed cured meats, variety of flavors

panels.title: The art of charcuterie
lines: A world of tradition, craftsmanship and flavor.
Charcuterie is the art of preserving meat through curing, smoking, drying and aging, creating unique textures, rich flavors and a lasting legacy across cultures.

plates.footer: Different lands, unique traditions, one table

corrections.should: Only the bellota grades (black and red label) are acorn fed, while cebo de campo (green label) and cebo (white label) Ibérico hams are raised on feed, so say acorn fed only when the label reads de bellota.
corrections.why: The Spanish Ibérico quality standard grades the ham by the pig's diet, and most Ibérico ham sold in the United States is cebo, not bellota.

corrections.should: Salami is the family name for fermented, dried sausages and its grind varies by style, fine in Milano but coarser in Genoa and loose in Felino, so it should not be taught as finely ground.
corrections.why: The plate lists soppressata, itself a coarse salami, as a separate card, and only the Milano style is notably fine.

corrections.says: Salumi Misti, Italy, Mixed cured meats, variety of flavors
corrections.should: Salumi misti is not a product but the Italian menu phrase for a mixed platter of cured meats, so it is a name for the whole board rather than an item on it.
corrections.why: Salumi is the family name for all Italian cured meats and misti means mixed, which the card's own caption states.

corrections.should: Wild Game is not a country or origin, and venison salami sold in the United States is made from farm raised deer, often New Zealand red deer, so tell guests it is farmed venison rather than hunted.
corrections.why: United States federal and state rules bar the commercial sale of wild harvested game, so any venison a restaurant buys is farmed and inspected.

corrections.says: Duck Breast, France, Silky, rich, unique
corrections.should: Plain duck breast names the fresh cut that is seared and served rosy, while the cured product on this board is duck prosciutto (magret séché), a salted and air dried duck breast sliced thin with its fat cap.
corrections.why: Every other card on the plate names a preserved product, and the picture shows thin cured slices with a fat cap, which is duck prosciutto or smoked duck breast rather than a raw breast.
